fields.title: Lamentations
fields.subtitle: Eikhah, “How!”
fields.description: Five poems of grief written in the ruins of Jerusalem after the Babylonians burned the city and its temple in 587 or 586 BC, named in Hebrew after their opening cry, “How!” Four of them are acrostics, running through the Hebrew alphabet as if to say this is suffering from first letter to last. The city weeps like a widow with no one to comfort her; the Lord has become like an enemy; children faint in the streets. And at the centre, a man who has seen affliction sits in the ashes and calls to mind that the LORD’s mercies have not failed: “They are new each morning; how great is your faithfulness!” Set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Lamentations?
qa.answer: A short Old Testament book of five poems mourning the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple by the Babylonians in 587 or 586 BC. Its Hebrew name, Eikhah, is its first word, a cry meaning “How!” The poems describe the siege and its aftermath without looking away, confess the people’s sin, complain to God and plead with him to look and remember. At the centre stands one of the Bible’s best-loved confessions of hope: “It is by the LORD’s loyal love that we have not been wiped out, for his mercies have not failed. They are new each morning; how great is your faithfulness!” (3:22–23).

qa.question: Who wrote Lamentations, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author. The ancient Greek translation introduces it as a lament of Jeremiah over Jerusalem, and Jewish and Christian tradition long followed this; English Bibles place it after the book of Jeremiah. Jeremiah lived through the fall of the city and is known to have composed laments (2 Chronicles 35:25). Many modern scholars think the poems come from one or more unnamed poets who witnessed the same events. All agree the poems were written soon after the fall of Jerusalem, by people who had seen it.

qa.question: Why is Lamentations written as an acrostic?
qa.answer: The first four poems are alphabetic acrostics: each verse, or in chapter 3 each group of three verses, begins with the next letter of the twenty-two letter Hebrew alphabet. The pattern made the poems easier to learn and to sing, and many readers think it also expresses completeness, grief told from A to Z, and gives order to an experience of chaos. The fifth poem keeps the twenty-two verses but drops the alphabet, as if the pattern itself has broken down while the prayer goes on.

qa.question: Where does the hymn “Great Is Thy Faithfulness” come from?
qa.answer: From Lamentations 3:22–23, translated here “They are new each morning; how great is your faithfulness!” The words are spoken by a man who has just described God’s hand against him in the bleakest terms, and who turns, with nothing in his circumstances changed, by calling to mind God’s loyal love and mercy. The hymn “Great Is Thy Faithfulness”, written by Thomas Chisholm in 1923, took its refrain from this passage.

qa.question: How is Lamentations used in worship?
qa.answer: Jewish communities read Lamentations each year on the fast of the Ninth of Av, which mourns the destruction of the first and second temples, and repeat its next-to-last verse at the end so as not to close on its final words. Christians have long read it during Holy Week, hearing in “Does it mean nothing to you, all you who travel this road?” (1:12) the voice of Christ in his sufferings. Its honest laments have also given many believers words to pray in times of grief.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Lamentations is poetry throughout, and each line is set on its own; “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
How the city sits alone that once was crowded with people! She has become like a widow, she who was great among the nations; the princess of the provinces is now put to forced labor.

— Lamentations 1:1

Lamentations is the Bible’s book of grief. Its Hebrew name, Eikhah, is its first word, a cry that means “How!”, and the word returns at the head of the second and fourth poems as well: how the city sits alone, how the Lord has covered Zion with a cloud, how the gold has lost its shine. The English name comes from the old Greek and Latin titles, which call the book the laments, or dirges.

It was written after the worst thing that had ever happened to the people of God. In 587 or 586 BC, after a siege of a year and a half, the Babylonian army broke into Jerusalem, burned the temple Solomon had built, tore down the walls and carried the people away. The city of David, the place where God had set his name, was a heap of ruins with jackals roaming over it. Lamentations is what faith sounded like in the rubble.

It is a short book, five poems in five chapters, and it is not easy to read. It describes famine and slaughter without looking away. But it has given the church some of its most loved words of hope, and it has given generations of sufferers a voice for what they could not otherwise say.

Five poems, and an alphabet

The first four poems are acrostics: each verse, or group of verses, begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Chapters 1, 2 and 4 have twenty-two verses, one for each letter. Chapter 3 has sixty-six, three for each letter, and stands at the centre of the book. Chapter 5 has twenty-two verses again, but the alphabet is gone.

Why write grief in alphabetical order? Readers have offered several answers. An acrostic is easier to learn by heart and to sing together. It also says something: this is suffering from A to Z, the whole of it, nothing left out. And it puts order around what has no order. When a world has collapsed, shaping the cry letter by letter is itself an act of faith, a refusal to let chaos have the last word. That the last poem breaks the pattern, while keeping its length, may be the most eloquent touch of all: the alphabet runs out, and the prayer goes on.

Many of the lines also move in a particular rhythm, a longer half-line followed by a shorter one, which scholars have linked with the funeral dirge. The book is meant to be heard as mourning.

Daughter Zion: the city weeps (Lamentations 1–2)

The first poem begins by looking at Jerusalem from outside, as a widow, a princess put to forced labour, a woman weeping through the night with “not one to comfort her”. That phrase, or something like it, returns five times in the chapter. Halfway through, the city herself begins to speak, and her words have been heard in Holy Week for centuries:

Does it mean nothing to you, all you who travel this road? Look closely and see whether any pain is like my pain, the pain that was brought on me, which the LORD laid on me on the day of his blazing anger.

— Lamentations 1:12

Zion does not pretend to be innocent. “The LORD is in the right, for I rebelled against his word.” Lamentations agrees with the prophets that the disaster was judgement, the curse of the covenant falling at last on a people who had been warned for generations. But it does not let that answer close the conversation. Knowing why does not stop the pain, and the poems say both things at once.

The second poem is harder still. Here the enemy who has torn down the city is named as the Lord himself: “The Lord has become like an enemy.” He has strung his bow, cast off his altar, wiped out the memory of festival and Sabbath. The poet watches little children faint in the squares, asking their mothers, “Where is there grain and wine?”, and he can find nothing to compare it to: “the breach in you is as wide as the sea; who could heal you?” He blames the prophets who told the city comforting lies and never laid bare its guilt. Then he urges the city to do the only thing left:

Get up and cry aloud in the night, as each watch of the night begins; empty out your heart like water before the Lord’s face. Raise your hands to him for the lives of your little ones, who grow faint from hunger at the corner of every street.

— Lamentations 2:19

The poem ends not with comfort but with a question flung at heaven: “Look, LORD, and take note: whom have you ever dealt with like this?” Lamentations is a book of prayer, and this is what its prayer sometimes sounds like.

The man who has seen affliction (Lamentations 3)

The third poem changes voice. Instead of the city, a single man speaks: “I am the man who has lived through affliction beneath the rod of his anger.” For twenty verses he describes what God has done to him, and he holds nothing back. God has walled him in, weighed him down with chains, shut out his prayer, waited for him like a bear in ambush, fed him wormwood. “My strength is gone, and so is all I hoped for from the LORD.”

And then, at the very centre of the book, with no change in his circumstances at all, he turns:

Yet I bring this back to mind, and because of it I will wait in hope: It is by the LORD’s loyal love that we have not been wiped out, for his mercies have not failed. They are new each morning; how great is your faithfulness! “The LORD is my portion,” I tell myself, “and so I will wait for him in hope.”

— Lamentations 3:21–24

Nothing outside him has changed. The city is still in ruins. What has changed is what he calls to mind. He remembers who God is: loyal in love, merciful, faithful, new every morning. The hymn “Great Is Thy Faithfulness” grew from these lines, and it is worth remembering where they were first spoken, by a man sitting in ashes.

The poem goes on to some of the deepest words in the Bible about suffering. “It is good to wait in silence for the LORD’s salvation.” “For the Lord does not cast people off for all time.” “For he does not bring affliction willingly or grief to human beings.” The Hebrew says, literally, that he does not afflict “from his heart”: judgement is something God does, but it is not what he delights in. Then the speaker becomes “us”, and leads the people in confession: “Let us look hard at the way we live and test it, and turn back to the LORD.”

Even so, the hope does not settle into calm. The poem returns to tears and to a pit with a stone over it, and the speaker remembers calling on God’s name “from the bottom of the pit”, and hearing him say, “Do not be afraid!” Many readers have heard in this man the voice of Jeremiah, who was lowered into a cistern; Christians have heard in him a greater sufferer still.

The gold grown dim (Lamentations 4)

The fourth poem looks back at the siege with a reporter’s eye. “How the gold has lost its shine!” Children who were worth their weight in gold are treated like clay pots. Princes once brighter than snow are blacker than soot and unrecognised in the streets. Mothers do what the covenant curses had warned of (Deuteronomy 28:53–57). Hope in Egypt’s help came to nothing; the king, “the very breath of our life, the LORD’s anointed”, was caught as he fled. And yet the poem ends with the first plain word of release in the book: “Your punishment is complete, Daughter Zion; he will not keep you in exile any longer.”

A people’s prayer (Lamentations 5)

The last poem is a prayer from first word to last, spoken by the whole community: “Remember, LORD, what has come upon us.” Its verses are short, and they list the losses of ordinary life under occupation: water bought for money, young men hauling millstones, elders gone from the gate, music fallen silent. Near the end it lifts its eyes to the one thing that has not fallen:

You, LORD, are enthroned forever; your throne stands through every generation.

— Lamentations 5:19

Then it asks God to turn them back to himself, and ends on a sentence so stark that synagogues, reading the book aloud, repeat the verse before it so as not to finish there.

Who wrote Lamentations?

The book does not say. The ancient Greek translation opens with a note that Jeremiah sat weeping and composed this lament over Jerusalem, and Jewish and Christian tradition long followed it; English Bibles still place the book after Jeremiah. Jeremiah did write laments (2 Chronicles 35:25), lived through the fall, and speaks often of weeping. Many scholars think the poems come from one or more unnamed poets who saw the same events, pointing to differences of style and outlook. Either way, the poems were written soon after the fall of the city, by people who had seen it.

Jewish communities read Lamentations each year on the Ninth of Av, the fast that mourns the destruction of both the first and the second temples. Christians have long read it in Holy Week, hearing in it the sorrow of Christ, who wept over Jerusalem and was himself despised and cut off.

How to read Lamentations

Read it slowly, and preferably aloud. It is short enough to read in one sitting, and is best read that way at least once, to feel its shape: grief, deeper grief, the turn to hope at the centre, grief remembered, and prayer.

Do not hurry to the hopeful verses. They mean what they mean because of where they stand. Lamentations teaches that faith can be honest about pain, and that complaint addressed to God is a form of prayer, not a lack of it. Here Scripture itself gives the sufferer words to say to God that most of us would not dare to say on our own.

And read it beside the rest of the Bible. Jeremiah and Ezekiel tell how the disaster came; Lamentations tells what it felt like. The Psalms of lament speak the same language. And the book of Isaiah answers its question, “Why do you forget us?”, with “Bring comfort, bring comfort to my people” (Isaiah 40:1).

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Lamentations is poetry throughout, and each line is printed on its own, as it is laid out in the Hebrew. The acrostic pattern cannot be carried into English, but the verses keep their shape: twenty-two to a poem, and sixty-six in the third.

“The LORD” and “the Lord.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, this translation writes “the LORD” in capitals; where it has the word for “master”, it writes “the Lord”. Lamentations uses both, sometimes in the same verse.

“Loyal love.” The Hebrew hesed, God’s faithful covenant love, is rendered “loyal love”: “It is by the LORD’s loyal love that we have not been wiped out.”

“Daughter Zion.” The poems personify Jerusalem as a woman, “Daughter Zion”, “Virgin Daughter Judah”, and this translation keeps the titles as they are, because the whole book is built on the picture of a bereaved city who weeps and speaks.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Lamentations 1
fields.body_html:
The city sits alone

How the city sits alone that once was crowded with people!
She has become like a widow,
she who was great among the nations;
the princess of the provinces is now put to forced labor.

Bitterly she weeps through the night, with tears on her cheeks;
of all her lovers there is not one to comfort her;
all her friends have betrayed her and turned into her enemies.

Judah has gone into exile after misery and hard servitude;
she lives among the nations and finds no place to rest;
all who chased her have caught her in the narrow passes.

The roads to Zion mourn, for no one comes to the festivals;
all her gates are deserted, her priests groan;
her young women grieve, and she herself is in bitter pain.

Her foes have become her masters, her enemies live at ease,
for the LORD has brought grief on her for her many rebellions;
her little ones have gone into captivity ahead of the foe.

All her splendor has gone from Daughter Zion;
her officials are like deer that find no pasture;
they stumble on without strength ahead of the hunter.

In the days of her misery and homelessness Jerusalem remembers
all the treasures that were hers in days gone by.
When her people fell into the foe’s hands and no one came to help her,
her foes looked on and laughed at her ruin.

Jerusalem has sinned greatly, and so she has become unclean;
all who honored her despise her, for they have seen her naked;
she herself groans and turns her face away.

Her skirts are stained with her uncleanness; she gave no thought to where she was heading;
her fall has been beyond belief, and there is no one to comfort her.
Look, LORD, at my misery, for the enemy has triumphed!

The foe has reached out his hand for all her treasures;
she has watched the nations enter her sanctuary,
the very ones you forbade to enter your assembly.

All her people groan as they search for bread;
they trade their treasures for food to stay alive.
Look, LORD, and take notice, for I am treated as worthless.

Is any pain like my pain?

Does it mean nothing to you, all you who travel this road?
Look closely and see whether any pain is like my pain, the pain that was brought on me,
which the LORD laid on me on the day of his blazing anger.

From on high he sent fire into my bones, and it overpowered them;
he spread a net to catch my feet and turned me back;
he has left me devastated and sick all day long.

My rebellions are bound into a yoke by his hand;
they are lashed together and laid on my neck; he has drained my strength;
the Lord has handed me over to those I cannot stand up to.

The Lord has cast away all the warriors within my walls;
he has summoned an assembly against me to crush my young men;
the Lord has trampled Virgin Daughter Judah as grapes are trodden in a winepress.

For all this I weep; my eyes stream, stream with tears,
for no one is near to comfort me, no one to revive my spirit;
my children are left forlorn, for the enemy has won.

Zion stretches out her hands, but no one comforts her;
the LORD has given orders against Jacob that his neighbors be his foes;
Jerusalem has become something unclean among them.

The LORD is in the right, for I rebelled against his word.
Listen, all you peoples, and look at my pain:
my young women and my young men have gone into captivity.

I called to my lovers, but they let me down;
my priests and my elders breathed their last in the city
as they searched for food to keep themselves alive.

Look, LORD, how distressed I am! My stomach churns;
my heart is overturned inside me, for I have rebelled so deeply.
Out in the street the sword takes my children; indoors there is only death.

People have heard my groaning, with no one to comfort me.
My enemies have all heard of my disaster and are glad that you have done this.
Bring on the day you announced, and let them become as I am!

Let all their wickedness come before you; deal with them
as you have dealt with me for all my rebellions,
for my groans are many and my heart is sick.

fields.title: Lamentations 2
fields.body_html:
The Lord’s anger against Daughter Zion

How the Lord in his anger has covered Daughter Zion with a cloud!
He has hurled the splendor of Israel down from heaven to earth;
in the day of his anger he gave no thought to the footstool of his feet.

The Lord has swallowed up without pity all the settlements of Jacob;
in his fury he has torn down the strongholds of Daughter Judah and brought them down to the ground;
he has dishonored the kingdom and its officials.

In blazing anger he has cut down all the strength of Israel;
he has pulled back his right hand in the face of the enemy;
he has blazed through Jacob like a flaming fire that devours everything around it.

He has strung his bow like an enemy, his right hand poised like a foe;
he has killed everyone who was a delight to see;
on the tent of Daughter Zion he has poured out his rage like fire.

The Lord has become like an enemy:
he has swallowed up Israel, swallowed up all its palaces, and laid its strongholds in ruins;
he has heaped up mourning and moaning in Daughter Judah.

He has torn down his booth as one strips a garden; he has ruined his place of meeting;
the LORD has wiped out the memory of festival and Sabbath in Zion,
and in his fierce anger he has spurned both king and priest.

The Lord has cast off his altar and disowned his sanctuary;
he has handed the walls of her palaces over to the enemy;
they raised a shout in the house of the LORD as on a festival day.

The LORD resolved to tear down the wall of Daughter Zion;
he stretched out the measuring line and did not hold back his hand from destroying;
he made rampart and wall lament; together they lie in ruins.

Her gates have sunk into the ground; he has wrecked and shattered her bars.
Her king and her officials are among the nations; instruction is no more,
and her prophets find no vision from the LORD.

The elders of Daughter Zion sit on the ground without a word;
they have thrown dust on their heads and wrapped themselves in sackcloth;
the young women of Jerusalem bow their heads low to the earth.

Weeping for my dear people

My eyes are worn out with weeping, my stomach is in turmoil;
my heart is poured out on the ground because my dear people are shattered,
as little children and babies faint in the city squares.

They keep asking their mothers, “Where is there grain and wine?”
as they collapse like the wounded in the city’s open squares,
while their life drains away in their mothers’ arms.

What witness can I bring for you? What can I liken to you, Daughter Jerusalem?
What can I set beside you to comfort you, Virgin Daughter Zion?
For the breach in you is as wide as the sea; who could heal you?

The visions your prophets saw for you were empty and worthless;
they did not lay bare your guilt to turn back your captivity;
the oracles they saw for you were hollow and misleading.

All who travel the road clap their hands at you;
they hiss in scorn and shake their heads at Daughter Jerusalem:
“Is this the city people called ‘perfect in beauty, the delight of the whole earth’?”

All your enemies open their mouths wide against you;
they hiss and grind their teeth and say, “We have swallowed her up!
It has come at last, the day we hoped for; we have found it, we have seen it with our own eyes!”

The LORD has done what he purposed; he has fulfilled his word, which he decreed long ago;
he has thrown down without pity;
he has let the enemy gloat over you and raised up the strength of your foes.

Their heart cries out to the Lord.
Wall of Daughter Zion, pour down tears like a torrent by day and by night!
Give yourself no relief; do not let your eyes rest.

Get up and cry aloud in the night, as each watch of the night begins;
empty out your heart like water before the Lord’s face.
Raise your hands to him for the lives of your little ones,
who grow faint from hunger at the corner of every street.

Look, LORD, and take note: whom have you ever dealt with like this?
Must women eat their own offspring, the little ones they cared for?
Must priest and prophet be slain in the Lord’s sanctuary?

Young and old lie on the ground in the streets;
my young women and my young men have fallen by the sword.
In the day of your anger you struck them down; you butchered them and did not spare.

As if calling a festival crowd, you summoned terrors against me from every side;
on the day of the LORD’s anger no one escaped and no one survived;
the children I nursed and brought up, my enemy has wiped out.

fields.title: Lamentations 3
fields.body_html:
The man who has seen affliction

I am the man who has lived through affliction
beneath the rod of his anger.
He has led me away and made me walk
in darkness, not in light.
Yes, it is me he strikes with his hand,
time after time, all day long.

He has worn out my flesh and skin
and shattered my bones.
He has built siege walls against me
and closed me in with bitter poison and hardship.
He has made me live in dark places
like those who died long ago.

He has hemmed me in, and I cannot get out;
he has weighed me down with chains.
Even when I shout and plead for help,
he keeps my prayer out.
He has walled off my road with cut stone;
he has made my paths twist.

To me he is like a bear waiting in ambush,
like a lion crouching in hiding.
He dragged me off the road and tore me to pieces;
he has left me devastated.
He has drawn his bow
and set me up as a target for arrows.

He has driven deep into my inner being
the arrows from his quiver.
I have become a joke to all my people,
the song they mock me with all day long.
He has fed me full of bitter things
and made me drink wormwood until I could take no more.

He has made me break my teeth on gravel;
he has trampled me down in the ashes.
My soul has been cut off from peace;
I have forgotten what good is.
So I said, “My strength is gone,
and so is all I hoped for from the LORD.”

Remember how I am afflicted and homeless,
the wormwood and the bitter poison.
My soul keeps remembering it
and is bowed low within me.
Yet I bring this back to mind,
and because of it I will wait in hope:

It is by the LORD’s loyal love that we have not been wiped out,
for his mercies have not failed.
They are new each morning;
how great is your faithfulness!
“The LORD is my portion,” I tell myself,
“and so I will wait for him in hope.”

The LORD is good to all who wait in hope for him,
to anyone who seeks him.
It is good to wait in silence
for the LORD’s salvation.
A man does well to take up a yoke
while he is still young.

Let him sit by himself and keep silent
when he has laid it on him.
Let him lie with his face in the dust;
there may still be hope for him.
Let him offer his cheek to the one who strikes him
and take his fill of insults.

For the Lord does not cast people off
for all time.
Though he brings grief, he will show compassion,
so great is his loyal love.
For he does not bring affliction willingly
or grief to human beings.
When all the prisoners in the land
are crushed underfoot,
when anyone is denied justice
in the presence of the Most High,
when someone is cheated in a lawsuit—
the Lord does not approve.

Who can speak and make it happen
if the Lord has not ordered it?
Do not disaster and good alike
come out of the mouth of the Most High?
Why should any living person complain,
anyone punished for their sins?

Let us return to the LORD

Let us look hard at the way we live and test it,
and turn back to the LORD.
Let us lift up our hearts as well as our hands
to God in heaven.
We have sinned and rebelled,
and you have not forgiven.

You have clothed yourself in anger and chased us down;
you have killed and not spared.
You have hidden yourself behind a cloud
that no prayer can pass through.
You have turned us into filth and rubbish
among the peoples.

Our enemies, every one of them,
have opened their mouths wide against us.
Panic and the pit have overtaken us,
ruin and collapse.
Streams of tears flow down from my eyes
over the destruction of my dear people.

My eyes pour out tears and do not stop;
they get no rest,
until the LORD looks down
and sees from heaven.
What my eyes see brings grief to my soul
because of all the women of my city.

People who had no reason to be my enemies
hunted me down like a bird.
They thrust me into the pit to end my life
and cast a stone over me.
The waters rose over my head,
and I said, “I am cut off!”

I called on your name, LORD,
from the bottom of the pit.
You heard my voice:
“Do not shut your ears to my plea for relief, to my cry for help!”
On the day I called to you, you came close
and said, “Do not be afraid!”

Lord, you have argued my case for me
and redeemed my life.
LORD, you have seen how I have been wronged;
give judgment in my case!
You have seen all their spite,
all their schemes against me.

You have heard their insults, LORD,
all their schemes against me,
what my attackers say,
and how they whisper against me all day long.
Look at them, whether they sit or rise:
I am the song they mock me with.

Pay them back, LORD, as they deserve,
for what their hands have done.
Give them a veiled and hardened heart;
let your curse be on them!
Chase them down in anger and destroy them
from beneath the heavens of the LORD.

fields.title: Lamentations 4
fields.body_html:
The gold has grown dim

How the gold has lost its shine, the finest gold has changed!
The sacred stones lie scattered at the corner of every street.

Zion’s precious children, once worth their weight in fine gold,
how they are now counted as common clay pots, the work of a potter’s hands!

Even jackals offer the breast and nurse their young,
but my dear people have become cruel, like ostriches in the desert.

The nursing baby’s tongue sticks to the roof of its mouth from thirst;
little children beg for bread, but no one shares any with them.

Those who once ate fine food lie ruined in the streets;
those raised in scarlet clothing now cling to the garbage heaps.

The punishment of my dear people is greater than the penalty for Sodom’s sin;
Sodom was overthrown in an instant, and no human hands were raised against her.

Her princes were brighter than snow and whiter than milk;
their bodies glowed redder than coral; they had the beauty of lapis lazuli.

Now they look blacker than soot; no one knows them in the streets.
Their skin has shrunk onto their bones; it has become as dry as a stick.

Those killed by the sword were better off than those killed by hunger,
who waste away as if stabbed, for want of food from the fields.

With their own hands, tender-hearted women have cooked their children;
they became their food when my dear people were shattered.

The LORD has carried his fury through to the end; he has poured out his burning anger.
He lit a fire in Zion, and it devoured her to her foundations.

The kings of the earth would not have believed it, nor would anyone living in the world,
that an enemy or attacker could march in through the gates of Jerusalem.

It was for the sins of her prophets and her priests’ guilt,
since they spilled the blood of the righteous in the midst of the city.

They staggered blind through the streets, so defiled with blood
that no one could touch their clothes.

“Go away! Unclean!” people shouted at them. “Go away! Go away! Do not touch us!”
So they fled and wandered from place to place,
and among the nations people said, “They cannot stay here any longer.”

The LORD’s own presence has scattered them; he will no longer look on them with care.
No respect was shown to the priests, no kindness to the elders.

Watching in vain for help

Our eyes still strained, looking for help that came to nothing;
from our watchtower we watched for a nation that could not save us.

They tracked our steps so we could not walk in our own squares;
our end drew near, our days were over, for our end had come.

Those who hunted us were quicker than eagles in the sky;
they chased us over the mountains, they set ambushes for us in the wilderness.

The very breath of our life, the LORD’s anointed, was caught in their traps,
the one of whom we had said, “Under his protection we will live among the nations.”

Rejoice and be glad, Daughter Edom, you who live in the land of Uz!
But the cup will be passed to you as well; you will get drunk and strip yourself bare.

Your punishment is complete, Daughter Zion; he will not keep you in exile any longer.
But he will punish your guilt, Daughter Edom; he will expose your sins.

fields.title: Lamentations 5
fields.body_html:
Remember what has come upon us

Remember, LORD, what has come upon us;
look, and see how we are put to shame.
Our inheritance has been handed over to strangers,
our homes to foreigners.
We have become orphans, with no father;
our mothers are like widows.
We have to pay money for the water we drink;
our own wood comes to us only at a price.
Our pursuers are at our necks;
we are worn out, and we are given no rest.
We pledged ourselves to Egypt
and to Assyria, to get enough bread.
Our fathers sinned, and they are gone,
and we carry the weight of their guilt.
Slaves rule over us,
and no one rescues us from their power.
We risk our lives to bring in our bread,
because of the sword in the wilderness.
Our skin burns like an oven
with the fever of hunger.
Women were raped in Zion,
virgins in the towns of Judah.
Officials were hung up by their hands;
no respect was shown to the elders.
Young men haul the grinding stones,
and boys stagger under loads of wood.
The elders are gone from the city gate,
the young men from their music.
Joy has gone from our hearts;
our dancing has turned into mourning.
Our crown has fallen from our head;
woe to us, because we have sinned!
Because of this our hearts are sick,
because of these things our eyes grow dim,
because of Mount Zion, which lies in ruins,
with jackals roaming over it.

The LORD is enthroned forever

You, LORD, are enthroned forever;
your throne stands through every generation.
Why do you forget us for all time,
and abandon us for so long?
Turn us back to yourself, LORD, so that we may return;
make our days new, as they were long ago,
unless you have rejected us completely
and your anger against us knows no limit.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Turn us back to yourself, LORD, so that we may return; make our days new, as they were long ago, unless you have rejected us completely and your anger against us knows no limit.

— Lamentations 5:21–22

Lamentations ends without an answer. Its last word is not a promise but a fear, that God’s anger might have no limit, and the prayer before it is left hanging. Jewish readers repeat the request to be turned back so as not to close the book on that note. But the book itself leaves it open, and that is part of its gift. It does not pretend that every grief resolves by the last line.

The question the book leaves with you

What do you do when God seems to have become your enemy? Lamentations does not offer an argument. It offers a practice. It names the loss in full. It confesses sin where there is sin, without pretending that the suffering is therefore small. It complains to God, to his face, and asks him to look. And in the middle of the ruins it calls to mind what it knows of him: that his loyal love has not run out, that his mercies are new each morning, that he does not afflict from his heart, that his throne stands through every generation.

The hope of chapter 3 is not a feeling that arrives when things improve. It is something the sufferer brings back to mind, deliberately, while nothing has improved at all. “The LORD is my portion,” he tells himself, “and so I will wait for him in hope.” That is a choice anyone can make in the dark, and the book shows a man making it.

Where the book points

The prayer “make our days new” did not go unanswered. Within fifty years exiles began to come home, and some seventy years after its destruction the temple was rebuilt. But Christians have also heard in Lamentations a deeper sorrow and a deeper answer. Jesus wept over Jerusalem and foretold its second destruction. He was the man who saw affliction under the rod of God’s anger, cut off, mocked all day long, laid in a pit with a stone over it, and raised. In him God has shown that he does not cast off for ever, and that the morning comes. The last book of the Bible gathers up the tears of Lamentations and promises a city where “Every tear he will wipe from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4).

Where to go from here

Lamentations is a small book, but some of the best devotional writing in this library has grown from its central chapter. A few places to begin:

  • On the mercies new every morning (Lamentations 3:21–24). Charles H. Spurgeon’s Evening by Evening, for May 28, on the memory that gives hope (3:21), and his Morning by Morning, for November 16, on the Lord as the soul’s portion (3:24).
  • On waiting for God (Lamentations 3:25–26). Andrew Murray’s Waiting on God, whose chapters “To Know His Goodness” and “Quietly” take these two verses as their text.
  • On suffering and the yoke (Lamentations 3:27–31). Spurgeon’s The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith, for January 12, “Love unto the End” (3:31), and September 11, “Sufferers Make Strong Believers” (3:27).
  • On prayer and self-examination (Lamentations 3:40–58). Morning by Morning again, for October 11 (3:41) and November 20 (3:58), Spurgeon on lifting up the heart with the hands and on the Lord who pleads the soul’s cause.
  • On waiting in silence. Portraits of Courage – Elisabeth Elliot, an Ochorus Original whose chapter “The Waiting Years” takes Lamentations 3:26 as its keynote.
  • On Lamentations and Christ (Lamentations 4:20). Augustine’s The City of God, Book XVIII, chapter 33, which reads “the LORD’s anointed” caught in the enemy’s traps as a word about Christ.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Lamentations in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather what the great writers of the church have said about each passage.

Then read Lamentations beside Jeremiah, who saw the disaster coming, and the Psalms, whose laments speak the same language. And keep it for the day you need it. It was written for people who had lost everything, and it has never stopped finding them. At its centre is a sentence that has carried more sufferers through the night than almost any other:

It is by the LORD’s loyal love that we have not been wiped out, for his mercies have not failed. They are new each morning; how great is your faithfulness!

— Lamentations 3:22–23
